sources.note: Original chapter in Puṣpikā, pp. 153-178, DOI 10.11588/hasp.1133.c15532. sources.title: Padmanatha Bhattacharya Vidyavinoda, Nidhanpur Copper-plates of Bhaskaravarman, Epigraphia Indica XII
sources.note: Original ASI edition, pp. 65-79, directly read as transcribed/OCR text on Jain Quantum. Discovery p. 65; Sanskrit opening p. 73 line 1, translation p. 76; camp p. 76; renewed charter p. 79 verse 28. No exact grant year or old editor’s disputed geographic reconstruction adopted. Modern normalized Devanagari and IAST reproduce the short Sanskrit opening, not seventh-century letter shapes.

sources.title: Padmanatha Bhattacharya Vidyavinoda, Two Lost Plates of the Nidhanpur Copper-plates, Epigraphia Indica XIX
sources.note: Original ASI edition, pp. 115-125, directly read through Jain Quantum text. P. 121 abridged translation supplies tax restoration, river accretions and seven shares for worship/oblation/hospitality; pp. 121-125 list grantees and Vedic affiliations. No claim that satra means a medical hospital. Family information is restricted to the named Brahman grantees.

sources.title: Silpisikha Baruah, Service groups in early Kamarupa society, 600 CE to 1200 CE (2019)
sources.note: Author-uploaded Indian History Congress conference paper directly read. Only Nidhanpur passages used: local officers, potter’s pit and metalworker Kaliya. Later ninth-century physician and fishing-tax evidence is excluded. The paper distinguishes occupation from automatic assumptions about hereditary caste.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India, The Mound and Ruins of the Stone Temple, Dah-Parbatia
sources.note: Direct ASI Guwahati Circle monument description. Doorframe is stylistically dated about the sixth century; its earlier date is explicit in the public card. Carved Ganga/Yamuna and floral bands are described directly. Later temple stages are not assigned to Bhaskaravarman.

proposedOverrides.name: Kamarupa
proposedOverrides.summary: A Brahmaputra-valley kingdom prominent in seventh-century diplomacy, with land grants and skilled craftspeople.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One exact missing historical-basemaps record, 600-700. No alias association with kamarupa-1200 or modern Assam. Date basis remains approximate map coverage; no fall at 700.
limitations: The broad polygon extends beyond the core Brahmaputra valley. The public opening warns that it does not prove control over every enclosed location.
Bhaskaravarman’s death around 650 and the uncertain transition do not end all Kamarupa history. Later evidence for Salastambha is retrospective.
The sixth-century Dah-Parbatia doorway is explicitly earlier context, not a securely attributed Bhaskaravarman commission.

Nidhanpur is a surviving renewal that itself mentions a burnt predecessor. No artificial exact year is attached. Old editors disagreed on the grant land’s precise location, so no modern locality is inferred from the vanished rivers.
Bana’s literary gift account is attributed as literature; legendary royal ancestry is distinguished from historical chronology.
Grantee families and Vedic affiliations do not imply universal literacy or schooling. No sufficiently specific contemporary medical or sanitation practice was established from the selected sources.
The Sanskrit phrase uses modern Devanagari and normalized transliteration; no original seventh-century glyph facsimile is claimed.
